content: Physical activity is essential for maintaining and improving human health. Engaging in regular physical activity helps prevent and manage a wide range of health conditions, enhances mood and sleep quality, increases energy levels, and supports healthy aging. Adopting a lifestyle that incorporates consistent physical activity is one of the most effective ways to improve overall health and well-being. Globally, one in four adults and four in five adolescents fail to meet the recommended levels of physical activity. Physical inactivity is a significant risk factor contributing to the global rise in obesity and noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). Each year, 4 to 5 million deaths could be prevented if global physical activity recommendations were met. In addition to insufficient physical activity, excessive sedentary behavior, such as prolonged sitting and screen time, poses a risk to health. Modernization and mechanization have made daily life more convenient, reducing the need and opportunities for physical activity. While technological advancements have brought many benefits, they have also contributed to a more sedentary lifestyle, which increases the risk of NCDs. Alongside unhealthy diets, tobacco use, and harmful alcohol consumption, physical inactivity is a major contributor to the growing global burden of NCDs. The Global Action Plan on Physical Activity 2018–2030, titled More Active People for a Healthier World, outlines strategies to promote physical activity worldwide. In the Pacific region, the NCD crisis is well-documented, and Pacific Island countries and territories have been actively addressing the burden of NCDs and their associated risk factors. Since the adoption of the NCD Roadmap in 2014, efforts have been made to tackle these challenges. The Pacific Physical Activity and Sedentary Behavior Guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the minimum levels of physical activity required to improve health outcomes and reduce sedentary behavior. For adults, engaging in at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week is associated with significant health benefits. Additional benefits can be achieved by exceeding these minimum levels. However, individuals participating in high-intensity or competitive sports should take precautions to prevent injuries. In the Pacific region, as in other parts of the world, many adults do not meet the minimum recommended levels of physical activity. Alarmingly, children and adolescents are even less active than adults, which is concerning as lifelong habits are often established early in life. Insufficient physical activity for adults is defined as less than 30 minutes per day on at least five days per week, or less than 150 minutes per week. For adolescents, insufficient activity is defined as less than an average of 60 minutes per day. The guidelines are based on the latest scientific evidence and are tailored to different age groups, abilities, and conditions. They emphasize the importance of reducing sedentary behavior, particularly among adolescents, who often exceed recommended limits for sedentary screen time. For example, adolescents averaging more than three hours of sedentary time per day are considered to exceed the recommended limits. The Pacific Guidelines are an adaptation of the World Health Organization's (WHO) global guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior. They were developed to support healthcare providers, workers, and policymakers in Pacific Island countries and territories. These guidelines serve as a foundation for health education and policy development, aiming to increase physical activity and reduce sedentary behavior to improve population health and prevent NCDs. The guidelines are informed by the updated global recommendations published by WHO in 2020, which were based on a comprehensive review of scientific evidence and global consultations. Similar conclusions have been reached in recent guidelines from New Zealand and Australia. The Pacific Guidelines also build upon the previous Pacific Physical Activity Guidelines for Adults, developed by WHO in 2008. Pacific Island countries and territories are encouraged to adopt or adapt these guidelines to promote physical activity and reduce sedentary behavior in ways that are culturally and contextually appropriate. While global recommendations are typically expressed in terms of weekly activity, the Pacific Guidelines provide daily recommendations to better align with local needs. Physical activity benefits the heart, body, and mind. Regular physical activity can prevent and help manage NCDs, reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety, and enhance cognitive function, learning, and overall well-being. Any amount of physical activity is better than none, and more activity provides greater benefits. For optimal health and well-being, adults should aim for 30–60 minutes of moderate aerobic physical activity on at least five days per week, while adolescents should strive for an average of 60 minutes per day.
